Last week I gave AI a set of practice questions from a well-known accountancy exam body. It scored 64%. A solid pass. 

I got 80%. 

Admittedly it cost me three hours and a broken nail to get there. AI did it in under three minutes. And six months ago, I doubt it would have passed at all. 

Some context. I've spent eighteen years in finance, most recently leading a UK FP&A team. Until the spring my AI skills extended as far as asking ChatGPT when to prune my roses (February, for those budding gardeners out there - pun fully intended). Then someone close to me had the patience to introduce me to Claude. I was hooked. I've since completed Imperial College Business School’s executive programme AI in Finance and I've picked up contract work training AI models. So I've spent six months looking at it from both sides: as a finance leader using it, and as someone paid to find its holes. 

Will it take our jobs? Not yet, in my view. It still gets things wrong. Sometimes spectacularly. 

I asked it to calculate my taxes and it concluded HMRC owed me a sizeable sum. I ran the numbers myself before booking the round the world trip. It turned out I was the one who owed the tax man. But the point is, I knew how to check the calculation and where the pitfalls could arise. 

As a junior analyst I once spent weeks preparing a beautiful presentation for our Commercial Team. I still remember wanting the ground to swallow me up when I presented customer growth of 4,017,893% in a declining market. The Commercial Director's sympathetic look as she told me to go away and relook at the numbers is etched in my memory. I'd made a simple Excel error and my formula had picked up the date from the header. Sixteen years later I can still remember the exact number. 

That isn't something you learn in a class. You have to have done it. Its scar tissue. 

Which brings me to the bit that worries me. 

Six months ago I'd have put AI at about the level of a part-qualified analyst. Today, I'd put it closer to an analyst with a couple of years experience. That's obviously subjective, and highly task dependent. But the rate of improvement is what concerns me. 

Meanwhile, the Big Four have reduced UK early-career hiring from previous levels. The reasons are mixed: a consulting slowdown, cost pressures, offshoring and, increasingly, AI. The exact weighting is debatable. The effect isn't: fewer people coming in, doing less of the manual work that taught the rest of us where the traps are. 

So how does someone learn to spot when AI is wrong, if they've never made the mistakes themselves? How do they think on their feet when a commercial director asks for their thoughts in a meeting, with no chance to go away and run the numbers? 

Which brings me to my question. For those who lead, recruit or train finance talent: What are you doing differently in this rapidly evolving world of AI? 

I'd love to hear what's worked, and perhaps more importantly - what hasn't?

There is so much noise out there and even here on LinkedIn about AI and it is created by AI itself.

Every day there's another headline, another benchmark, another multi-billion dollar model release. If we you ask most leaders what AI they use, and they'll rattle off the same names: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen.

But as a CTO, CIO, or COO, your job is not to chase that noise but to filter it out and solve real problems.

Having worked and deployed production grade AI, most often the right tool for most enterprise jobs is not the massive general-purpose LLM at all. It's a smaller model trained for exactly one task and it beats the big model on every metric you actually care about: speed, cost, accuracy, and privacy.

Why? Because specialization beats generality when the job is defined. For example:

- SmolLM3 or Phi-4 Mini: Is for everyday logic and reasoning tasks. Why pay per-token API fees and send your data to a third party when a small model runs locally, responds in milliseconds, and costs nothing per request?

-StarCoder2 or CodeGemma: for code completion inside your org. Developers' code is some of your most sensitive IP. Running a code model in your own environment means it never leaks to an external API.

- LayoutLMv3: for extracting data from forms, invoices, and contracts. It's trained to read documents the way humans do I.e understanding layout, tables, and field positions  so it doesn't guess, it just reads.

- Whisper or Kokoro: for speech-to-text and voice. Customer calls contain personal data. Local voice processing means that data never leaves your infrastructure.

-Fine-tuned BERT: for routing and classification: tagging support tickets, filtering emails, sorting documents. These models are tiny, run in milliseconds, and cost pennies a day. A general LLM doing this job is like hiring a surgeon to put on a bandage.

Notice the pattern: every one of these solves a specific, recurring business problem. None of them need to write poetry.

Big general models are still valuable, they're great for prototyping, brainstorming, and tasks that genuinely need broad knowledge. But real enterprise AI that  cuts costs, protects data, and actually works in production is built from specialized tools.

Stop using a sledgehammer when you need a precision tool.

#Oldie_but_Goldie - What happens when your company spends months building a solid AI policy — governance committees, approval workflows, risk registers, ethical guidelines, but your vendors operate outside all of it?

The uncomfortable truth is that your vendors could be deploying models that touch your data, influence your customers, and expose you to risk, all outside your (or in fact any) governance framework.

And if something goes wrong, your board, your regulators, and your clients won’t care whose system failed. The liability traces back to you.

That’s the blind spot some organisations are only now starting to recognise.

▪️Common Blind Spots in Vendor AI Governance:

#1 Policy vs. Practice - Your vendor's contract says "we use AI responsibly." But what does that mean?

Who audits their model training data for IP infringement or unauthorised scraping?

What bias testing happens before deployment?

Is there version control when models get updated mid-contract?

Most agreements are silent on these questions. You're trusting assurances with no verification mechanism.

#2 The Sub-Processor Chain - Your vendor uses AI. Their cloud provider uses AI. Their data processor uses AI for quality checks.

You have zero visibility into that chain. Yet you carry the liability if something breaks, bias in hiring decisions, data leakage, regulatory non-compliance.

#3 Incident Response Theatre - Standard contracts promise "prompt notification of AI system failures." Sounds protective. But ask yourself:

What qualifies as a failure? Model drift? Bias above a threshold? Hallucinations in outputs?

What's "prompt"? 24 hours? 30 days?

Who decides when something is material enough to report?

Without definitions, you get notification when it's too late to mitigate.

▪️Some useful things to demand in your next SLA or vendor contract:

Training Data Transparency - Require vendors to disclose data sources and confirm licensing rights. Include audit provisions.

Model Testing Cadence - Mandate bias, accuracy, and security testing at defined intervals.

Incident Definition & SLAs - Define what constitutes an "AI incident" (bias metrics, accuracy drops, security events). Set notification windows: 24-48 hours for material issues.

Sub-Processor AI Mapping - Require vendors to disclose which sub-processors use AI and for what purpose.
 
Right to Audit AI Systems - Not just data processing, but model performance, training practices, and governance controls.

Make sure your AI governance doesn’t stop at your company’s walls. Your vendors need to be part of it too.

Too expensive to compete with small teams. Too small to compete with the giants.
That's where most service firms are today.

It happened before. The New York Times went from 1.1 million readers in 2002 to more than 13 million subscribers today. The Dallas Morning News went the other way, from about 520,000 to around 61,000. And Lenny Rachitsky, an ex-Airbnb product manager writing a newsletter on his own, has over a million.

When the internet made distribution free, newspapers didn't shrink evenly. A few giants got bigger, a lot of small one-person publications appeared, and the middle got squeezed.
I think the same is now happening to every service business that grows by hiring people. Law firms, agencies, consultancies, software houses.

When the work gets cheap, the market splits:
- On one side, a few very big players. Brand, big contracts, and money to put AI into everything.
- On the other side, a lot of very small teams. One to five people, AI doing most of the production, selling a result instead of hours.

...and in the middle, the 50–300 person firm selling people by the month. Stuck in between.

Law already shows it. Big firms just had a record year billing hours. At the same time, new AI startups sell a contract review for a fixed price of about £95. The top and the bottom are doing fine. The pressure is in the middle.

Under my last post about software houses dying, someone left a smart comment: when his seniors got faster, they didn't bill fewer hours, they started to own a bigger piece of the product. That's the way out of the middle, I think. You become a small team that owns results, or you grow into a big one that owns a whole category.

Today I'm a company of one, and it's on purpose.

Newspapers had 10 years to see it coming. Most of them didn't. Service firms have maybe 2–3. So what will separate the firms that make it from the ones that are already too late?

Graduates keep asking, "Will AI take my job?"

At last week's AI and careers panel at ECU, I told the room to start asking employers a different question: "You've brought AI into the business. What are you going to do for your grads?"

Employers are walking into graduate interviews expecting grads to have the answer: "AI can do a lot of this job now, so how are you going to use it?" That's backwards. Hiring a grad and then throwing them into AI with no guidance is antithetical to the very purpose of a graduate program.

So flip the script. Whether you're clerking, interning or weighing up graduate offers, ask them:
 → How are you training your people to use AI properly?
 → Who supervises how it gets deployed here?
 → How will I build real expertise if AI handles the entry-level work?

You're giving them your time and your skills. Choose the place that's going to invest in you.

A few other things we got into on the night:
📈 AI hasn't replaced lawyers. It's creating work for them. Now that anyone can generate a contract or lodge a claim with AI, there's more poorly drafted material in the system, and someone has to respond to it. I'd expect the same pattern in a lot of professions.

🎨 Creativity matters more now, not less. The most valuable people will combine technical skill, commercial sense and genuine human insight. They'll build solutions that deliver ROI, connect emotionally with the people using them, and are creatively delivered, with the brand, tone, design and experience customers expect.

Huge thanks to Senali Madugoda Gunaratnege and Edith Cowan University for hosting, Josh T. and Dr Eunice Sari at the Western Australian AI Hub for organising, and my fellow panellists Ron Forlee, Dr Yulianna Shiikha and Joanna Jones. It was a great conversation with a sharp, engaged audience.

To any grads reading this: you have more leverage than you think. Use it!

New UK data suggests AI is denting job prospects for computer science and economics graduates, with entry-level technical hiring falling. Graduate schemes were never the only route into technical work, and in a city this size they are the least available one.

Five alternatives worth working through:

1. Early-stage local companies, before they advertise. Small teams hire when the work appears, not when a recruitment cycle opens. Follow what they are building and send something specific about it.

2. Contract work into local employers. Plenty of organisations around Lancaster have a single piece of data or software work that never justifies a permanent post.

3. Research-adjacent roles. Research software engineering, data tooling, analysis. These posts exist within universities and the projects attached to them, and they often go to people already in the room.

4. A side project somebody pays for. One paying user is evidence, and it interviews better than a tutorial build.

5. Turning up where hiring actually happens. In a small ecosystem, a lot of roles get filled through someone who already knows you can do the work.

None of these is quicker than a graduate scheme. They are just more available here.

Your AE might not have a sales problem but they might have a buying "committee" problem.

One of the biggest changes in Learning & Work isn't simply what companies are buying.
 👉 It's who gets involved in the decision.

Learning technology used to be largely an L&D conversation.

Increasingly, it's also a conversation involving:
 💻 IT
 💷 Finance
 🤝 Procurement
 ⚖️ Legal
 🔒 Security / Compliance
 😃 Senior business leaders

And that changes what “good selling” looks like.

A great AE can't just build a relationship with the L&D buyer and run a compelling demo.

They need to be able to multi-thread/approach.
Build an internal champion.
Understand different stakeholder priorities.
Create a business case.
Navigate risk and procurement.
And keep momentum when the person who loves the product isn't necessarily the person who signs the contract.

 👉 That's a very different commercial skillset.

And it should make us question something:
 ❓ Are Learning & Work companies still hiring AEs for the buying process they had five years ago?

 🗣️ Because if the buying group has changed, the salesperson you need may have changed too.
This is particularly relevant as AI pushes learning further into core workforce workflows and where the conversation becomes less about “training” and more about productivity, skills, transformation and business outcomes.

For Founders and Commercial Leaders:
 ❓ Has the profile of your ideal AE changed as your buyers have changed?

Meta is building an enterprise sales org for its AI stack. The hire matters more than the product list.

Meta Enterprise Platform will sell the Muse agent, Meta Business Agent, Muse API and Muse Code to businesses and developers. It reports to Zuckerberg through an incoming chief enterprise platform officer: the CEO and President of MongoDB, previously product and engineering leadership at Cloudflare and nearly eight years at ServiceNow including President and COO.

Read that résumé as the actual announcement. An enterprise platform is not a product. It is the wrapper around one: APIs, agent runtimes, admin controls, SLAs, security review artefacts, and a sales and support organisation that lets a company run a vendor's AI inside its own systems. Enterprise revenue comes from that wrapper, not from model quality. Meta is importing the wrapper rather than promoting from its consumer side, which tells you where it thinks its gap is.

The reporting line is the second signal. Enterprise deals priced inside an advertising P&L get subordinated to it. A direct line to the top is how a platform company avoids that, and it is the usual reason platform companies under-invest in enterprise sales in the first place.

For buyers, this adds a fourth credible conversation alongside incumbent SaaS and cloud vendors. More options pressure pricing and shorten proof-of-concept cycles. For developers on Muse API and Muse Code, distribution is consumer-scale but the enterprise support model is unproven. Procurement teams should ask for contractual security and privacy commitments, not blog assurances.

The counterweight: naming a platform and hiring a well-credentialed leader is not shipping one. The facts describe intent to turn the stack into deployable products, not generally available enterprise offerings. Meta's privacy record gives procurement a reason to wait for guarantees.

So watch for the artefacts, not the announcement: first named enterprise customers, published SLAs, data-residency and security documentation, GA dates for Muse API and Muse Code. Until those exist, treat this as a hiring and positioning signal. The metrics that follow will shift too, from engagement to deployment contracts, and that is what analysts and competitors will start judging Meta on.

Unpopular opinion: most growing companies don't need "more HR software." They need less of it, switched on at the right time.

Here's the pattern we kept seeing before we built ZenSkayl Workforce OS:
📊 At 10 people: a spreadsheet works fine.
📊 At 30 people: the spreadsheet has 7 versions, and nobody knows which leave policy applies to whom.
📊 At 50 people: you buy an all-in-one suite, pay for 20 modules and use 4.

So we went the other way. You start with the core and add modules only when the pain shows up:
• Leave chaos? Add Leave Management, with separate rules and approval chains for each policy.
• Shift teams working across sites? Add Shifts, with swaps right from the mobile app.
• Hiring ramping up? Add a full ATS that's already connected to your employee data.

You're billed only for what's active, and there are no binding contracts.

降りてくるコンサル、上がれない開発。FDEはどちらから育つか / Consultants move down, developers struggle to move up. Where will FDEs come from? （English follows）

9月、FDE（Forward Deployed Engineer）の育成プログラムの発表が相次いだ模様です。SES・SIer向けに「今いるエンジニアを、AI案件を提案し実装できる人材へ」とうたうものや、FDE検定まで出てきました。
一方、NTTデータ子会社のフォーティエンスコンサルティングは「FDE型コンサル」で5年後に売上100億円を目指すとのこと。業務知識を持つコンサルタントが、実装へ守備範囲を広げていると報じられています。

FDEには、開発から上がるルートと、コンサルから降りるルートがありそうです。

SI企業の営業部門と話すと、どこもOffering型への変革を掲げています。元来受託のビジネスは、要件に正確に応える人材を集めて強くなってきました。市場分析、提案、パッケージ販売とは求められるものが違います。育成で埋まる差ではなく、海外のようにM&Aや人の入れ替えで動かすのも難しいと感じています。

逆に、コードを書くことはAIで代替できる部分が増えている。上流から降りてくる方が可能性は高そうです。ただ、AIエージェントも含めて、開発の工程と品質を最後まで回すPMスキルがコンサル側で育っているのかは、私には知見がありません。コンサル会社はブランドと給与水準も高く、人も集めやすいので新規獲得するのかもしれません。

まさにFDEをどう実現するかの議論ですが、皆様はどのようなアプローチで進めていますか？

---

In September, several FDE training programs launched in Japan. One for SI firms promises to turn current engineers into people who can propose and build AI projects. There is even an FDE certification exam. At the same time, Fortience Consulting, an NTT DATA subsidiary, aims for 10 billion yen in sales in five years with "FDE-style consulting." Consultants with business knowledge are moving into building.

So there are two roads to FDE. Developers moving up, and consultants moving down.

Every SI sales team I talk to says they are shifting to an offering model. But contract firms originally grew by hiring people who answer requirements well. Market analysis, proposals, and package sales need different people. I feel training cannot close this gap, and M&A or replacing people is hard in Japan.

Meanwhile, AI can now do more of the coding. So moving down from consulting looks more likely. But I do not know if consulting firms are growing PMs who can run development, process and quality, including AI agents, to the end. Consulting firms have strong brands and high pay, so they may simply hire them.

This is really about how to make FDE work. What approach is your company taking?

Five months ago I joined an ML outsourcing team to run delivery on a generative AI platform. This week the contract wrapped up, so here is what those months looked like.

The platform generates music, video and images, with an LLM assistant and a recommender system on top. Sixteen people across five ML streams, coordinated through their tech leads. My side was scope, data dependencies, quality gates and model licensing. The modelling itself was the engineers' job.

Two things stand out.

The first was cost. We were running inference on dedicated GPUs and the bill showed it. I analysed the spend, ran the evaluation of alternatives with the teams, agreed the switch with the client and saw the migration through. Around $40K a month saved, at comparable volume and output quality.

The second was reliability. I prioritised that work with the tech leads and introduced postmortems that made ownership between vendor and client explicit. Over a month the team brought the error rate on assistant requests down from 2.2% to 0.036%, and orchestrator p95 latency from 5.9 to 4.1 seconds.

The client has now paused development, and my contract ended with it.

The delivery part of this was familiar ground. Before AI I spent four years at a digital agency in Moscow, the last three heading its e-commerce development department: four PMs, a portfolio of 15+ concurrent projects, and the department's P&L. In my final year revenue grew 14.5% with gross margin holding at 50%.

Different domain, same job: complex delivery, cross-functional teams, and someone accountable for the number at the end.

Now I am looking for what comes next. Full-time or consulting, remote from Tbilisi or with relocation. Delivery management, project portfolios, AI/ML programmes, e-commerce.

Recruiting is getting faster. But the moment people can actually start contributing often isn’t.

AI and automation can accelerate sourcing, screening and matching. Yet after the match, the pace can change quickly.

Approvals take time. Contracts move between systems. Onboarding follows a separate process. Training and scheduling start only after hiring is complete.

The friction has shifted.

For companies managing ramp-ups, changing volumes, multiple locations or cross-border workforce needs, a shorter time-to-hire only goes so far if time-to-productivity remains unchanged.

The underlying issue is often not recruiting itself. It is the disconnect between recruiting and deployment.

Demand, skills and availability may already be visible. But if that data does not connect with approvals, onboarding, scheduling and operational requirements, speed gained at the beginning is lost further down the process.

Workforce transformation therefore cannot stop at faster matching.
It needs to connect the entire journey: from identifying the right skills to making people available and operationally ready where and when they are needed.

For us, this means looking beyond filling a role and focusing on the friction between demand, matching and actual deployment.

👉 Where does your organisation lose the most time today: finding the right people or getting them ready to contribute?

What does Andy Burnham's firstThe Labour Party Conference speech mean for UK workers, and those looking for it? Here's what he said, what we think will change, and what was left out.

To those working in care: "You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you." 🩺
He said care workers look after people while on "poverty pay," and apologised that politicians had let them down for so long. The government is admitting care work is underpaid - a new National Care Service (NCS) could give the job more. But until then, no pay rise, no figures, and the service won't start until the next Parliament. Yes, it's recognition, but not reward.

To those working for the NHS: "We have let you down too."
The argument: fixing social care eases pressure on the NHS - fewer people stuck in hospital beds, less "corridor care." Should help staff eventually, not quickly.

To young people: "It's not your fault. It's ours." 🎓
Almost a million young people are not working or studying. Burnham made sure to show he blames the system, not them. More support is coming - with strings attached.

The big theme: "working-class aspiration."
More talk of "good growth in every postcode." Outcomes remain to be seen.

What could actually change:

New routes into work for young people - technical and academic pathways from age 14, treated as equally valuable. A 45-day work placement at 16-18, then an apprenticeship at 18, and no more long waits for mental health support. The most concrete jobs policy in the speech - but it only works if employers actually sign up. Financial pressure, living-wage needs, and AI-driven cost-cutting sit at odds with that ambition. 🤖

Cheaper travel to work - a £2 bus fare cap across England from January, through 2027. 🚌

Jobs across the country - rebuilding regional industry, a new publicly owned Great British Grid, government contracts favouring British business, a "Number 10 North." Together, a push for jobs outside the usual hotspots. Childcare infrastructure wasn't part of this picture - and it needs to be.

AI - Britain will use its G20 presidency to push for global AI rules. But the speech said almost nothing about how AI is already changing jobs, skills and hiring today. No sign of intent to safeguard jobs as companies turn to AI and automation.

What's missing: 🔍
For anyone in work or looking for it, three questions matter: how do I get in, how do I get on, and will I be paid fairly? This speech answered the first. On wages, the minimum wage, pay transparency, the gender pay gap, or the Employment Rights Act - nothing. That silence stands out, especially since the same speech raised care workers' poverty pay.

That is what the buying signals agent in QuikSignal reads. Every night it goes through six job boards, SEC EDGAR, the US Federal Register, company newsrooms and public award notices for the accounts you watch, scores what it finds against everything else that week, and shows you the document behind each one.

What it changes:

- You see the role a company advertised before the budget conversation, not after it
- A rule with an effective date tells you when an obligation starts, which is a date you can plan around
- Every signal opens its own source, so a rep can check it before they send

- It does not buy intent data and it does not de-anonymise your website visitors. Every signal is an event somebody put out, and you can open it yourself.

Myth: "OCR is solved. Document AI is just ChatGPT on a PDF."

Reality: companies still drown in invoices, contracts, KYC packs, and scanned forms — and they hire people who turn it into trusted structured data.

The role: Document AI / Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) Engineer.

Not a chatbot job. Not batch OCR alone. You own the pipeline: layout + OCR → classify → extract → confidence / validation → human exceptions → handoff into ERP, claims, or finance. GenAI raised the ceiling; accuracy, cost, and audit trails still need an owner.

India hiring signal (titles vary):
• Document AI / Applied Science — extraction, grounding, LLM eval (Thomson Reuters, Bengaluru)
• Generative AI / Document Intelligence Engineer — OCR + GenAI at scale (TCS, Bengaluru)
• Graduate Trainee / IDP Associate — OCR workflows, ABBYY / Otera-class tools, Python + JS (Siemens, Bangalore)
• AI Engineer, Document Intelligence — invoices, POs, contracts + ERP integrations (Veltriance, Hyderabad)

Why now: Mordor Intelligence pegs IDP at ~USD 3.17B in 2026, with Asia-Pacific the fastest-growing region. IDC notes GenAI extraction and early agentic IDP workflows — trust and ROI still decide who ships.

Skills that keep showing up:
• Python + data/API engineering
• Document AI stacks (Azure Document Intelligence, Textract, Google Document AI — or LayoutLM / Donut-class models)
• Field-level eval: F1, straight-through rate, cost per page
•  Bonus: VLMs, PII handling, exception queues

Starter project (one weekend):
Label 40–60 public invoices. Build classify → extract 8–10 fields → confidence flags → score vs a gold set. Ship the notebook + a short failure gallery (skew, stamps, handwriting).

How to demonstrate: public repo with metrics, not a vibe demo. This lane buys measurable extraction quality.
